summary: Describes CATNIP, a proposed common architecture for the network layer, meant to let IP, CLNP and other protocols interoperate. It was submitted to the IPng effort and is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: One plan for a shared language that several different kinds of networks could all understand.

subtitle: A unified network layer format that bridges IPv4, CLNP, and IPX

tldr.problem: The 1990s Internet faced multiple incompatible network layer protocols: IPv4, OSI CLNP, and Novell IPX, making it difficult to operate a seamless global network and complicating the move to a next-generation IP.
tldr.mechanism: CATNIP defines a common network datagram format with a 16-byte fixed header that can represent and translate between different network protocols. It uses cache handles for fast routing and optional address omission for header compression.
tldr.outcome: CATNIP was a proposal for IPng (IPv6 work) but was not selected for deployment. The Internet eventually adopted IPv6 (RFC 2460) instead, which uses a different architecture. CATNIP is Historic.

today: RFC 1707 is Historic. CATNIP was a candidate proposal for IPng (the next-generation Internet Protocol), submitted to the IETF's IPng working group. The community ultimately selected IPv6 (RFC 2460), which uses a different architecture based on a simpler fixed-size header and different address format. IPv6 did not attempt to unify with CLNP or IPX in the way CATNIP proposed. The decline of CLNP and IPX networking in the late 1990s made convergence on multiple protocols less urgent.

sections.title: The Multiple-Protocol Problem
sections.content:
In the early 1990s, the Internet ecosystem supported multiple network layer protocols, each with its own addressing scheme and datagram format. IPv4 was the dominant Internet protocol, but OSI's CLNP was standardized for international networking, and Novell's IPX was widely deployed in local area networks. This fragmentation created operational complexity.

Network administrators had to support multiple routing protocols (BGP for IPv4, IS-IS for CLNP, and proprietary protocols for IPX), multiple address spaces, and translation mechanisms between them. The move to next-generation IP (IPng) risked further fragmentation unless a unified approach could be found.

CATNIP's core objective was convergence—bringing all three protocols under one roof without abandoning any of them. Rather than deprecate CLNP or IPX, CATNIP proposed a common format that could represent addresses and datagrams from any of the three in a uniform way. This would allow transport protocols like TCP and UDP to operate over any network layer without modification.
sections.plainLanguage: Three big shipping companies each have their own way of writing addresses and wrapping packages. This proposes one common way that works with all three so a package doesn't need unwrapping every time it changes hands.

sections.title: The CATNIP Datagram Format
sections.content:
The CATNIP datagram begins with a fixed 16-byte header, followed by variable-length destination and source addresses, options, and then the payload data. The fixed header contains:

  • NLPID (8 bits, value 70 hex): identifies the datagram as CATNIP (labeled as IPv7).
  • Header length (8 bits): allows headers up to 1020 bytes.
  • Flags (8 bits): including DAO (destination address omitted), SAO (source address omitted), RFD (report fragmentation done), MRO (mandatory router option), and ERS (error report suppression).
  • Time to Live (8 bits): hop limit, decremented by at least 1 per hop.
  • Forward Cache Identifier (32 bits): a handle passed forward by routers to identify routing decisions and enable address omission.
  • Datagram Length (32 bits): total length up to 4 GB.
  • Transport Protocol (16 bits): identifies TCP, UDP, or other protocols.
  • Checksum (16 bits): IP-style header checksum.

The variable address fields that follow can be omitted if the FCI field is valid and the DAO/SAO flags are set, allowing significant header compression on subsequent packets in a flow.
sections.plainLanguage: The CATNIP header is 16 bytes and contains basics like where the packet is going, how far it can travel, and a shortcut number so routers don't have to write out full addresses on every hop.

sections.title: Addressing: A Unified NSAP Scheme
sections.content:
CATNIP unifies addressing around a variant of the OSI NSAP (Network Service Access Point) format, with an Authority and Format Identifier (AFI), Initial Domain Identifier (IDI), and Domain-Specific Part (DSP). This scheme can represent IPv4, CLNP, and IPX addresses by using different AFI values.

IPv4 addresses are mapped with a new AFI (document uses 192, to be assigned by IANA) and an Administrative Domain (AD) number. The entire existing IPv4 address space is represented as AD 0.0, allowing transparent mapping of existing 4-byte IPv4 addresses into the NSAP format (7 bytes total including length and AFI).

CLNP addresses (already in NSAP format) map directly with no transformation.

IPX addresses map using AFI 47 with the Novell ICD (International Code Designator), representing a 4-byte network number plus 6-byte MAC address in the DSP.

Future IPv6 (called SIPP at the time) addresses would use AFI 192 with AD 0.1 and the 128-bit SIPP address as the DSP.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of each protocol's addresses as a last name: IPv4 is 'Smith', CLNP is 'Jones', IPX is 'Brown'. CATNIP writes them all with a common format that says what last name each is, then the actual address.

sections.title: Stateless Translation Between Protocols
sections.content:
A key strength of CATNIP is that translation between network protocols happens stateless: no mapping tables, no database lookups, no special border routers. Instead, addresses are transformed using simple algorithmic rules.

When a CATNIP-capable router receives a CLNP datagram intended for a destination reachable via IPv4, it converts the CLNP header to CATNIP format, translates the IPv4 destination address to CATNIP NSAP form, and sends the datagram forward. The reverse translation is equally straightforward. No router needs to consult any external state.

This design allows incremental deployment with zero configuration changes: a CATNIP system can be inserted anywhere in the network topology, replacing an old IPv4 or CLNP router, and existing systems will continue to operate without modification. Over time, as systems upgrade, they can take advantage of the unified format for improved performance, but there is no moment where everything must change at once.

For datagram forwarding, CATNIP uses the Forward Cache Identifier (FCI) field. Each router that processes a datagram may place a hint in the FCI field identifying the next hop, based on routing protocol feedback or explicit routing information. The next router can then use this hint to accelerate its routing decision and, if appropriate, omit source and destination addresses from subsequent packets in the same flow (with DAO and SAO flags set).
sections.plainLanguage: Translation happens with simple math, no magic tables. A router can translate IPv4 to CATNIP and pass it along without asking permission or checking a database. And if routers agree on where traffic is going, they can leave out the addresses to make packets smaller.

sections.title: What CATNIP Does and Does Not Define
sections.content:
CATNIP deliberately defines only the core: the datagram format and addressing. It intentionally does not specify routing protocols, error handling protocols (ICMP/CNLP), naming systems, autoconfiguration, or multi-hop multicast routing. These are considered out of scope, to be addressed by existing protocols (IS-IS for CATNIP routing, ICMP for error reporting, DNS for naming).

The design accommodates multiple modes of operation. For connectionless service, systems use full addresses on every datagram (DAO and SAO flags clear, FCI zero). For circuit-like service, routers can establish an FCI handle for a virtual circuit, allowing address omission on subsequent packets. For flow-based service, the FCI can represent a locally significant flow identifier, similar to IPv6 flow labels.

This flexibility means CATNIP can support any intermediate model between full connectionless datagrams and connection-oriented circuits, all within the same packet format and over the same routers.
sections.plainLanguage: CATNIP defines the envelope and the address labels. It doesn't say how to pick the best route (that's IS-IS), how to report problems (that's ICMP), or how to find addresses (that's DNS). Other systems handle that.

fields.name: NLPID
fields.desc: Network Layer Protocol ID; value 70 (hex) for CATNIP.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: DAO, SAO, RFD, MRO, ERS bits plus reserved bits.

fields.name: TTL
fields.desc: Time to Live; decremented per hop.

fields.name: Forward Cache ID
fields.desc: Routing hint set by routers to enable address omission.

fields.name: Transport Protocol
fields.desc: TCP (6), UDP (17), or other transport protocol number.
